children.text: In 2002, Martin Fowler codified fifty-one foundational patterns in
(PoEAA). While technologies, programming languages, and cloud topologies have evolved radically over the subsequent decades, the core tension of enterprise software engineering remains unchanged:
how do we organize complex business rules so that changes remain predictable, invariants remain strictly enforced, and data integrity is guaranteed?

In modern distributed microservices and serverless stacks, teams frequently abandon structured architectural layering under the guise of agility. The consequence is predictably disastrous: business validation scattered across React frontends and API gateways, database entities treated as simple bags of state, and procedural controllers spanning thousands of lines.

In this first installment of our four-part deep dive, we re-examine Fowler’s foundational architectural patterns through the lens of modern TypeScript and Domain-Driven Design (DDD). We explore the mechanics of strict unidirectional layering, navigate the trade-offs along the Domain Logic Continuum, define the boundaries of the Service Layer, and eliminate Primitive Obsession using self-validating Value Objects.
The bedrock of enterprise architecture is the division of software into three primary layers:
: Handles user interaction, HTTP request parsing, authentication tokens, serialization/deserialization, and view formatting.
: The intellectual heart of the system. Contains business rules, domain invariants, calculations, workflow validations, and domain events.
: Manages interactions with external infrastructural mechanisms: relational databases, document stores, message buses, search indexes, and third-party APIs.

body.alt: The Three-Layer Architecture showing Presentation Layer, Domain Layer, and Data Source Layer with strict unidirectional dependency flow.
body.caption: The Three-Layer System: strict unidirectional dependency flow with zero inward coupling.

children.text: The domain layer must never depend on the presentation layer, and the domain layer must not be coupled to the concrete storage mechanics of the data source layer.

When the domain layer is kept pure—free from HTTP request objects, framework decorators, and raw database client imports—it becomes trivially testable in isolation. Unit tests can execute in milliseconds with zero mocking of database connections or network sockets.
Common Layering Violations in Modern TypeScript

: Importing an ORM entity (e.g. TypeORM, Prisma, or Mongoose schema) directly into an API controller, exposing persistence-specific annotations and auto-generated database columns directly to the network.
: Placing calculation and validation logic inside custom SQL queries or repository helper methods, fragmenting business rules between application code and database stored procedures.
: Calculating financial balances, discounts, or permissions in UI client components rather than enforcing them as domain invariants in the backend.
How should domain logic be structured within the application? Fowler outlines three primary architectural patterns, which represent a spectrum of complexity:
Pattern  ·  Mental Model  ·  Best Suited For  ·  Maintenance Risk
·  Procedural scripts handling one request from start to finish  ·  Simple CRUD, batch jobs, ETL, internal tools  ·  Severe duplication and scattered validation as rules grow
·  Single class per database table/view operating on recordsets  ·  Data-centric apps with tabular recordset tooling  ·  Inability to represent complex polymorphic domain models
·  Network of objects encapsulating state and behavior  ·  Complex business logic, state transitions, invariants  ·  Higher initial cognitive overhead and mapping cost

A Transaction Script organizes business logic into a single procedure that handles a single request from the presentation layer. It makes database queries, validates input, executes calculations, and writes updates directly back to storage.

Popularized during the desktop and early web era (particularly with Microsoft ADO.NET and DataSet architectures), the Table Module pattern provides a single class per database table or view. Unlike an entity in a Domain Model, an instance of a Table Module has no individual identity—it operates on tabular data collections.
While rare in modern object-oriented TypeScript backends, its intellectual descendant appears in columnar data processing pipelines (such as Pandas, Apache Arrow, or BigQuery BigFrames).

In a Rich Domain Model, the business domain is represented by an interconnected graph of objects. Each entity encapsulates its own data and provides methods that guarantee its invariants can never be violated. Outside code cannot mutate private fields; state transitions occur only through explicit business operations.
3. The Coordinator: The Service Layer Pattern

A critical challenge when adopting a Rich Domain Model is deciding where the boundary of the application lies. If domain entities only encapsulate their own business rules, who handles transaction rollback, database retrieval, external payment gateways, and event dispatch?
This is the purpose of the
The Service Layer defines an application's boundary with a layer of services that establishes a set of available operations and coordinates the application's response in each operation.

body.alt: The Service Layer as Workflow Coordinator establishing transaction boundaries and coordinating domain entities with infrastructure.
body.caption: The Service Layer coordinates transactions and infrastructure without bleeding domain calculations into procedural scripts.

children.text: Avoiding the Anemic Domain Model Anti-Pattern
In 2003, Fowler identified the rampant misuse of the Service Layer: the
Entities are completely hollow: mere bags of public getters and setters with zero methods.
All business logic, conditional validations, calculations, and state checks are extracted into gigantic procedural
This is simply a Transaction Script masquerading as an object-oriented architecture.
: "Can this plan be upgraded given the current status? How much credit is refunded?" (Pure logic, no I/O).
: "Fetch the customer, initiate database transaction, invoke the entity's upgrade method, process the payment charge, save to DB, send confirmation email." (Coordination and I/O).

solves this by encapsulating value semantics:
: Once created, its internal state cannot be modified. Any mathematical operation or transformation returns a brand new instance.
: Two Value Objects are equal if their attributes are equal, not because they share an in-memory pointer or synthetic database ID.
: The constructor or factory method validates all invariants upon instantiation. An invalid Value Object can literally never exist in memory.
5. Production Case Study: SaaS Subscription & Proration Engine

To demonstrate these patterns working in harmony, we implement an enterprise SaaS subscription engine. The application must support mid-cycle plan upgrades, calculating unspent balance from the old plan and prorating the charge for the remainder of the billing period.

body.alt: Hands-On Architecture: Enterprise SaaS Subscription & Proration Engine sequence and component interactions.
body.caption: Hands-on workflow: Service Layer orchestrates I/O while Value Objects and Entities enforce pure domain invariants in memory.

children.text: The aggregate root protects state invariants. Notice how the calculation of proration credit and plan assignment is performed entirely by domain methods, keeping business rules inside the domain layer.
The service layer coordinates between the repositories, payment gateways, and domain entities. It does not calculate proration math itself; it delegates to the entity and handles side-effects.
: Keep domain entities isolated from frameworks, databases, and HTTP transports to ensure high velocity and testability.
Match Complexity to the Domain Continuum
: Use Transaction Scripts for simple tabular pipelines; transition to a Rich Domain Model when business rules, lifecycle state, and calculations become non-trivial.
: Keep the Service Layer thin. It coordinates transactions, external I/O, and persistence, but delegates core calculations and state transitions to the aggregate entities.
